title: Humility
hook: humility is taking your rightful space, no more and no less

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mendel of Satanov's method: one trait a week, a short line by day, a mark at night. Today, the first trait on a walk through his kind of list.

Two people in the same meeting. One talks through every pause, takes every credit, fills every silence. The other sits in the corner with the answer everyone needs and never says it, because who are they to speak? Ask the room which one is humble, and the corner may well get the vote. Jewish teachers of character would push back: both have the measure wrong. One takes too much space. The other takes too little, and the room loses what they had to give.
screen: `ONE FILLS EVERY SILENCE.` → `ONE NEVER SAYS THE ANSWER.` → `BOTH HAVE THE MEASURE WRONG.`

segments.voice: Anavah. Humility. Four turns. First, Moses. The Torah, in the book of Numbers, calls Moses very meek, more than anyone on the face of the earth. That's the same Moses who stood before Pharaoh, carried the tablets down the mountain and argued with God on behalf of his people. So humility here doesn't mean shrinking. The humblest man in the Torah's own description took up a great deal of room, when the room needed him. Second, the prophet Micah. Asked what God requires, he answers with three things, and the last is to "walk humbly with thy God." Walk: humility as a way of moving through the world, not a feeling about yourself. Third, two pockets. A story is told about the Hasidic teacher Rabbi Simcha Bunim. He said a person should carry two slips of paper, one in each pocket. One says: for my sake the world was created, a line from the Mishnah. The other: I am but dust and ashes, Abraham's words in Genesis. The trick is knowing which pocket to reach into. About to stay silent while someone is wronged? The first. About to take more than your share? The second. Fourth, the measure. That's why some Mussar teachers describe anavah as being right-sized: not too large, crowding everyone out; not too small, hiding a gift the room needs. A humble person, in this picture, thinks accurately, then makes room for others. Humility makes a good first trait, because every other trait needs it to stay honest.
screen: `MOSES: VERY MEEK, AND NOT SMALL.` · `WALK HUMBLY: A WAY OF MOVING.` · `TWO SLIPS, TWO POCKETS.` · `NOT TOO LARGE, NOT TOO SMALL.` · then, large: `RIGHT-SIZED.`

segments.voice: Start with your body: let your seat be just what you need, feet on the floor, back long, shoulders easy. Picture your next conversation and ask which pocket you'll need: if you usually swallow something true, picture saying it plainly; if you usually take over, picture leaving one pause open for someone else. If you pray, carry this before God in your own words; if not, simply sit right-sized, and let that be enough.
Anavah. Humility: in Mussar, being right-sized, taking the space that is yours, no more and no less. Today's word.
Your line: right-sized. Not too large to crowd others out, not too small to give. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Mussar practice, Jews working on anavah watch how much space they take in conversations and in their homes, sometimes keeping the two-pocket teaching of Rabbi Simcha Bunim as a reminder.

chat.says: If Moses was the humblest man, why was he always arguing and leading?
options: Humility isn't shrinking: Moses took up room when his people needed him.
Because the Torah calls him meek only before Pharaoh, never after.
Because humility only counts in private, not in front of a crowd.
chat.meaning: Numbers calls Moses very meek, yet he stood before Pharaoh and argued with God for his people: humility as right-sized, not small.

notes: Micah 6:8 quoted as 'walk humbly with thy God' (JPS 1917, same in KJV); confirm.
Numbers 12:3 paraphrased ('very meek, more than anyone on the face of the earth'); 'the humblest man in the Torah's own description' rests on that verse. Confirm.
Simcha Bunim's two slips told as 'a story is told'; the lines are paraphrased from Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 and Genesis 18:27.
'Some Mussar teachers describe anavah as being right-sized' reflects contemporary Mussar teaching (e.g. Alan Morinis's phrasing); confirm it is fair and not too tied to one teacher.
